utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Can the witness please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Zaric, good morning.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaric, I'm going to examine you very briefly with regard to certain details from your statement. The Court decided that you should come here and speak viva voce about these details. We have already talked about the way in which you should give evidence here, that you should wait for me to put my question, that you should then, after a few seconds, answer the questions so please make a pause so that the transcript would reflect everything that we've said. Let me just tell you one more thing. Everybody here is aware of your health condition, so if you do not feel well at any point, please do not hesitate to tell us. Just tell us, please. Could you please tell me your name and surname for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Fatima Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours I provided a sufficient number of redacted copies of witness's statement so maybe this can be distributed to the Trial Chamber. I already gave one copy to the Prosecution so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaric, you have already given your statement. It is already part of the case file. I would like to ask you something now. Let us restrict your statement, your testimony, to the 16th of April, 1992 only. You already said that you were at your friend's birthday party. After that, you went to close your shop, and take care of the books there. Then you went home. After that, your two sons came. After that, your husband also came, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So sometime around 11.30, you went to bed. Can you tell us what happened then, in your apartment, whether there were any telephone calls, who called? Could you please tell the Court about this?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. That night, that evening, I was at a restaurant. We were celebrating the birthday of my friend Nusreta Besirevic. I stayed perhaps until 8.00. The other members of the party remained and I went to the shop where my son Denis worked. I completed the paper work that I was supposed to take care of that day. I put all the money together. I tidied the store and around 9.00 I went home, which was the usual thing I did every day. Perhaps a few minutes later, or a few minutes before 9.00, my sons returned home. It was a bit strange. I found it a bit strange why they came so early. When I asked them how come they were being so nice and good and how come they came home so early, they said the cafes are half empty, there were very few people in town. While I chatted with my sons, not much time went by, my husband also came, Simo Zaric. We watched TV. Simo was in a very good mood. He said that although he never drinks alcohol he said to me, "Wife, I've had a glass of brandy." We laughed. Our sons went to bed. Simo and I stayed up some more. I don't know what we talked about. The telephone rang and I answered it. Nobody said anything to me from the other side of the line. That didn't surprise me, because at that time, before that, I had been receiving anonymous calls, even threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Zaric. Now, tell me, nobody spoke to you over the phone and did you go to bed after that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: We went to bed after that. We didn't even fall asleep. It was perhaps about 11.30, we didn't even fall asleep. Again, the phone rang. Simo went to the phone. When he returned, I asked him who it was, and he said to me that they were calling him from the SUP, the duty policeman, Luka, who I knew from before, because he had been a policeman for quite a while in Samac before the war. I asked what he wanted, and he said that he had asked Simo whether he knew that they had received information that some military personnel with white ribbons were moving about Tisina, a village near Samac. Simo immediately called Stanko Djurdjevic who lived in Tisina, and he talked to him. I asked him what did he say to you? He said that nothing was going on and that they'd see in the morning. Simo called the SUP again, and informed the duty policeman about what Stanko Djurdjevic had told him. We went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let me summarise. First Mr. Gregurevic called your husband?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After that, he called this --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Stanko Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Stanko Djurdjevic and then again he called Luka Gregurevic and informed him about what he learned from this man Stanko?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Now, tell me, did you go back to bed?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we went back to bed and we fell asleep. I was already nervous because I knew that I had to get up early to go to work. Again, the phone rang. It woke us up. It woke me up actually and I was trying to wake Simo up and I was saying, "Simo this could only be a call for you."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I didn't want to interrupt you but did Mr. Zaric answer the phone then again?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, he did. I was angry. I didn't know what was going on in Samac. He didn't know either. He said that this call was from the command of the 4th Detachment. It was the person who was on duty there who called him. I don't know. And that he informed him that some gun fire could be heard in town but in a different part of town, not near our building. I got up. We went to the terrace or actually Simo was already on the terrace. And I stood at the door. Shooting could be heard. Nothing different from what could have been heard before that, because there had been times when there had been shooting. He said that he had to call Radovan Antic and he did. I panicked. I was afraid. After having talked to Antic, he said to me, "I have to go." He put on his suit. He took his weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment, Mrs. Zaric. A suit can mean in our language different things. When you say "suit" are you referring to military clothing or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to military clothing, a military type suit, olive grey, and he took his weapon and he took the car keys. I saw him off. I heard him ignite the car and off he went from the yard. When he left, it was only then that I really panicked. I didn't know anything. I tried to phone my mother's house. The phone wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, after these conversations that Mr. Zaric had with Antic, and the people at the command of the detachment, at one point, the telephone ceased to operate?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The telephone was my only means of communication with my family and I have a lot of family members in Samac. However, it was not working. Around 5.00, the phone rang. Perhaps it was after 5.00. I cannot give you the exact time because a lot of time has gone by in the meantime. The phone rang so I was really happy to hear that it meant that the phone started working again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Madam. Because of my coughing, the interpreters could not hear the end of what you were saying. They could not hear the end of your answer. I do apologise. The last thing that was recorded in the transcript was that you were actually pleased and happy that you heard the telephone ring because it meant that it started working again.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, so when the phone rang that morning around 5.00, around 5.00, tell me who was on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: It was Simo. He said to me, "Wife, the situation in town is complicated. I have to go with Radovan to Pelagicevo. Don't go anywhere from the house. I'll call when I get back."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, did you go by what your husband said? Did you stay at home? Did you not leave the house?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did not. I stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, around 8.00 approximately or perhaps a bit earlier, a bit later, did you receive a telephone call again?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, Simo called me and said that he had returned, that he was at the command, that the children and I should not leave the house, and that he would come home when he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Madam, we have now come to the 17th of April, the morning of the 17th of April, did your husband come home?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Simo came, the children were already up, they did not know what was going on. They don't -- they didn't know that Simo and I were getting up, that he spoke on the telephone, and that he was on the terrace, et cetera. I told them about all of that and I was very serious about it and I said we are going to wait for Daddy to come and then we are going to discuss it. He did indeed come. It was about 9.00 or 10.00. He was uneasy, upset. I asked him whether he wanted to eat something and he said, "No, I don't have time. I have to go back to the command." And then he said to me that that day, that morning, a Crisis Staff was being established. I didn't even know what a Crisis Staff was, because I had never been in a war. I had no idea what kind of formation this was, what its tasks were. He spent very little time at the house, and he said, "Do not leave the house at all." And we went by that. I was afraid for my older son because he was older, he was already of age, whereas the younger one, Miran [as interpreted], was under age. We stayed. The only means of communication with Simo was the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let's just correct one thing in the transcript. Your younger son's name is Mirel, right?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, his name is Mirel and my other son's name is Denis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Madam, we are still on the 17th of April. You said that your husband stayed at the house for a while and that then he left again. Did he tell you where he was going?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: He told me that he had the task of assigning the members of the 4th Detachment next to the bank of the Sava River and Bosna River. And again, he emphasised that we should not leave the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me whether on the 17th of April, apart from this arrival in the early morning hours, whether Mr. Zaric came by the house during the day at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No. He did not. He did not even spend the night at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us now talk about the 18th of April. We have already covered this part in your statement so we don't want to repeat saying that the military came in front of your house, members of the 4th Detachment, asking for illegal weapons to be surrendered. We will skip that part. We just want to know whether you saw your husband on the 18th of April, whether he came, if he did how long did he stay?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That morning, members of the 4th Detachment came. The apartment next to mine was empty. My neighbour Biljana, a Serb, left for Serbia earlier on. So that it was only me with my children who was there on that particular floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did they knock at your door as well?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. First they knocked at the door of Biljana's apartment but nobody answered so they knocked at my door. I didn't allow my children to open the door. I went out. They asked us whether we had any weapons, and I said, yes, my husband has weapons but he is not at home, he took all the weapons with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell them that your husband is the assistant commander of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what their reaction was?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, they were very polite, they weren't violent. They didn't go into the house. I spoke to the other neighbours, they didn't enter anyone's apartments. Those who had weapons and who weren't members of the 4th Detachment volunteered and surrendered their weapons of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did Mr. Zaric come home sometime during the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: He telephoned me on the 18th and he said that their headquarters would no longer be in the building where they were situated earlier on. The command of the 4th Detachment. But that they would be relocated close to our building with our neighbour who had this very fine house, next to Jovo Dusanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Is this Mrs. Zaric the part called the plum orchard, Sljivak?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We -- on the 19th and the 20th of April, did you see your husband and, if so, how often, how would he arrive? Did he spend the home at night -- did he spend the night at home?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came. He was very tired. I told him, "Well, you should lie down. Look, you look very tired." So he did not spend the nights there. He spent the nights at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you about what was going on in the town?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. But he spoke very little about it because I am quite fearful by nature and I was very afraid. I was afraid for my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what he told you to the extent that he told you anything?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, he told me that the Crisis Staff was formed, that now we had the Serbian Municipality of Samac, that some Special Forces arrived. We called them the many-coloured ones. That the 4th Detachment did not have the role that was originally envisaged. They started rounding up people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, when you said they started up rounding people, you were speaking of the 4th Detachment first?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was the police who started rounding up people, arresting them. I don't know what the criteria was but I know that these were people who were of non-Serbian ethnicity and Simo took it -- it was very difficult for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether Simo told you something to the effect that some of the members of the 4th Detachment were also arrested by the police?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They arrested people who had weapons belonging to the 4th Detachment, even though they were in possession of papers for these weapons and I don't know who gave them these papers, how they came by these papers but these people ended up in prison. Among them was the husband of Simo's sister. He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, let us now turn to another event, which took place I think on the 21st of April, when your husband came home. Can you tell us why is -- why was this particular day different from the others?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. On this day, this was a day of both fortune and misfortune. My husband suffered a great deal, for the fact that he did not side with or sympathise any national party, political party, and he suffered also for the fact that he did not distinguish people by their ethnicities. He also suffered for the fact that he had me as a wife, a Muslim, who was later on called Balinkura, a Turk, everything else that they called me all sorts of different names but never used my own name, never called me for what I was. He arrived and he was visibly upset. He was almost malformed in his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you feeling fine, Madam?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Please continue, then.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I asked Simo what is going on? He told me, "Today, you have to leave Samac with the children." I said no. We will share our destiny. He said, "No, you have to go. Stevan Todorovic and the Special Forces which arrived from Serbia were harassing him at SUP, swearing him, his communist mother, his wife, Balinkura, they were telling him to forget all about brotherhood and unity. They were pushing the gun barrels into his mouth. By nature, he was courageous, honest and proud. That particular day he was humiliated by the very people who wanted to destroy everything and everyone who did not share their opinion. They humiliated all people from all different ethnicities, Croats, Serbs and Muslims. This threat that was given to my Simo by Stevan Todorovic and by those of his yes-men, I took it very seriously, they said that they would kill me and my children and everything that was -- and everyone who were members of my family, and Simo's family. I had no choice. I decided, although with great difficulty, to leave my husband behind, to leave my brother behind, my family, and I have many members of my family in Samac, my friends, and my neighbours. And secretively, it was just before nightfall, with my friend Mico Vidovic, I literally disappeared from Samac with my two sons. It was very, very difficult for me. I cried. I was sorry to leave my brother, who had suffered a lot in this war, because we were brought up by a family, by parents, who never taught us to hate other people for the mere fact that they were not members of our ethnic group. My parents taught us to respect people by what they were -- by their worth and not by their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaric, you said, I disappeared from Samac, literally disappeared. Can you tell us how you actually left Samac with the help of this friend?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: He came with his car in front of our house. No one knew. It was -- they took us to Tisina, where there were other refugees. It was in the evening. It was dark. It was cold. I didn't take any of my clothes with me. I opened the cupboards and I saw -- closets and I realised that whatever I did take would be just too much. So I just took off in my gym suit which was a bit torn, and I didn't even take any of the diplomas, school certificates of my children, myself, because I thought that I would come back, which didn't help. There were other people there who I didn't know. It was dark there. This was a closed-type truck, where I sat with my children and perhaps it was -- I was lucky to have left that day because on that particular day, the border was still open for all ethnicities. Everyone could cross the border. Had it been a few days later, I am positive I would not have been able to leave. We arrived late in Belgrade, at my sister's, and my brother-in-law's. This encounter -- this encounter of ours was really terrible because we cried, all of us. I cried, my sister, my brother-in-law, and I don't know what these tears actually meant, whether they meant happiness or sadness. I think both actually. My mother was in Gradacac. My sister was in Gradacac, where she lived. My brother remained in Samac. I didn't know what happened to Simo's parents [as interpreted]. Everyone was leaving any way they could and the family literally disintegrated in a few days' time. This was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour I believe I need one small clarification for the transcript because here on page 13, line 7, the witness said I didn't know what happened to Simo's family. Because here it says parents and Mr. Zaric's father was already dead by that time. This was just that small intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaric, in your statement, which is already part of the case file, you said that already on the 23rd of April, 1992, you were registered as a refugee?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I was registered at the insistence of my brother-in-law. We went to the Red Cross. He drove us in his car and my two sons as well, and we were registered with the Red Cross in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you just wait a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while proofing with this witness yesterday, she informed me that she brought her refugee ID. So I would like to be tendered into evidence. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now we do have only B/C/S version. It is already given -- it is already given for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The point is let me ask the Prosecution, is it contested that she registered as a refugee by the Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no need then for us to produce this certificate of registration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaric, in the rest of your statement, it's clear from what you say when you returned to Samac, so we will not go into those details again. I would just like to put a few questions to you now that refer to some previous testimonies before this Tribunal. First of all, for the sake of clarification, when you said that your mother remained in Gradacac, and your sister too, can you tell us where Gradacac is?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Gradacac is some 18 or 20 kilometres away from Samac. My sister lived in Gradacac. My mother was visiting her. We didn't know that war would break out. Had we known, we would not have separated. We would have stayed together. We tried very hard to get my mother out, for several months, but she was unable to return to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Madam, during the war, which side of the warring parties was in control of Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: It was the Muslims, Gradacac was a predominantly Muslim town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will now put a few questions to you following from the testimonies of some other witnesses before this Tribunal. Tell me, in brief, whether Mr. Blagoje Simic and Mr. Miroslav Tadic ever came to your apartment before the war, before hostilities broke out?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Madam, in the shop you owned, did you sell automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I may conclude from your reply that you did not sell a Kalashnikov to a certain Bahrija Vajzovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't like weapons. I have never held a weapon in my hand. I don't know anything about weapons. I can only distinguish between a rifle and a pistol, and that's all. And if my lawyer hadn't asked me, I wouldn't have known who this man was. I know that he comes from Samac but I never knew his name. His real name, I only knew his nickname. In Samac, everybody had a nickname, and that's what we knew each other by.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I will ask you another question that has to do with your statement. Does the name Jevrosima mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I read in Dragan Lukac's book -- I read in a book -- he didn't want to attack me, he wanted to represent my husband as a Serb nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But did you change your name Fatima into Jevrosima?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I never changed my name. I'm not ashamed of my name. And my Simo would never want to do that. I'm proud of my name. I'm proud of my family. I'm proud of my parents and my ancestors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to ask a few more questions and then we will conclude. In Belgrade, you were a refugee staying with your sister and your brother in law?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During this period, while you were a refugee, did somebody else from Bosanski Samac come and stay in that flat?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as far as you can recall, who lived in that apartment during the war?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: There were 16 of us in a one-room flat. We slept on the floor. We were very crowded. And we had no idea how people from Samac got hold of our address, looking for a place to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us the names of the people who stayed there, as far as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: The people who spent the longest time there were Satka Jasarevic; her daughter, Fata; Salko Ceribasic; Fadil Mustafic; Fatka Mustafic; Adin Mustafic, their son; Jasna Mustafic, their daughter in law; and Anja Mustafic, their daughter, Jasna and Dina's daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Judging by the last names, I would say that these were all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Jasarevic family that you mentioned, the lady and her daughter, were there related to Osman Jasarevic, also known as Roma?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, Satka Mustafic was his mother, Roma's mother and Fata was Roma's sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You said Mustafic, did you mean Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I meant Jasarevic, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a brief period in private session and I will complete my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaric, I have concluded your examination-in-chief. My learned friend will now put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have finished examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Zaric, my name is Di Fazio, I will ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I hope I won't be too long in my questions. We can speed it up if you give brief answers as well. Mrs. Zaric, your husband has had long experience as a policeman and in the security services, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In fact, he was chief of the SUP in Bosanski Samac, I believe, for four years, from 1975?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There followed a period of his involvement in private enterprise, working for companies, and then in 1985, I believe, he became a senior inspector in the state security service? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: He wasn't involved in private business. He continued working in a state-owned company, in the business sector, but not as a private entrepreneur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get that correct. I'm not interested in that period. But in fact, after that period of working with the companies, he became a senior inspector in the state security, and that was in September of 1985, I believe. Am I correct? I'm sorry, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And he rose from the position of senior inspector in the state security to the position of chief of the state security in Modrica and he was responsible for the areas of Modrica, Odzak and Samac, correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And he only retired from that job as chief of security -- state security, in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So some six years in charge of the state security services covering an area which included of course the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in that position, right up until about seven months before the outbreak of hostilities in Bosanski Samac, if my calendar calculations are correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And of course, in that position as chief of state security, he had access to good, high level intelligence relating to all sorts of activities in those areas that I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much he knew and who he contacted because this is a secret service and people don't talk about things like that at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I understand that you weren't doing his job and you were not in state security and I'm not suggesting that you had access, chapter and verse, to everything that he knew. However, from your discussions with him, it was apparent to you, wasn't it, that he had good access to good intelligence for those areas?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Your husband was also a man who was interested in politics and in fact had joined, for a long period of time, the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the League of Communists. I was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Of course. And many other people in the former Yugoslavia were members of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Exactly, precisely. But he was also interested in politics, was he not?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: It's not only that he liked politics. He liked sports too. He liked folklore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I know about that. I've read his interviews and I understand that he's a man of wide interests but my question is?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He was interested in politics as well, was he not?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Politics was an integral part of his job. He was supposed to be informed about many things, and he could only know about these things from these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That makes good sense, with respect, Mrs. Zaric. In -- it would be fair to say that he followed politics at a national level and also followed politics at a local or municipal level?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: What do you mean at a national level? I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, he kept abreast of political developments in Yugoslavia, he kept abreast of political developments within the municipality, within the areas of Odzak and Samac and the other -- the third area that he was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, he followed Bosnia and Herzegovina more than Yugoslavia, because his headquarters were in Sarajevo, not in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And he -- sorry, I withdraw that. Let me rephrase it. In your discussions, in your talks with your husband, it was clear, wasn't it, that he was a man who was well aware and following carefully the activities of the national parties in Yugoslavia and in particular Bosnia and Herzegovina, the HDZ, the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: It's not that he only followed that. Ordinary people followed it too. The establishment of national parties, I think that already at that time there came a period of uncertainty when coexistence became more difficult among us who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that he was in some way obsessed with the politics of the national parties. All I'm suggesting is that your husband was a man who was right up to date, right up to date, well informed, about the policies and developments of the national parties, the Croatian -- HDZ, the Muslim SDA and the Serb SDS. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Your husband was also a man who was well known in Bosanski Samac and in -- indeed in the other municipalities close to the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He knew a lot of local politicians, including members of the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We socialised with people, with individuals, we paid no attention to ethnic or religious background. We were not interested in that. Neither he nor I had any sympathy for the national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fair enough but that's not really with respect my question. My question is that he socialised and knew well many members of these national parties, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know which period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period in late 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had contacts with them. He didn't have any points in common, but he said hello to them. He didn't turn his head away from anyone, no, but he didn't socialise with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And he particularly in early 1992, he attended many meetings in the municipality, meetings at which local politicians from those national parties were present? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know where and when he attended meetings with people. It would be too much for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand that and I'm not asking you to provide details of each and every meeting, nor dates, nor occasions. My question is a general one. In early 1992, he attended many meetings, didn't he, at which local politicians were present, to discuss local politics and other issues?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an accurate answer to that question. It's not that I don't want to. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your husband, in early part of 1992, spoke on behalf of the 4th Detachment and spoke of -- at meetings, of -- well, I'll restrict my question to that. Spoke on behalf of the 4th Detachment at meetings, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: He probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't actually know, you're speculating or that you do know that he attended --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I think he did, I think he did. I think he did speak on behalf of the 4th Detachment because wherever he would appear, he could only speak that way because he was assistant commander for information, security and information. So if he was invited anywhere, he certainly went, and he could not speak on behalf of any national party. He could only speak on behalf of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And there were growing ethnic tensions in Bosanski Samac in -- well, in late 1991 and early 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So all of that meant that he had to have an extremely clear, good idea of the -- knowledge, I should say, of the policies of the national parties, including the policies of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Certainly. We as a family, my husband, we all had to pay a price for this. He retired prematurely because he did not want to become a member of the SDS although offers were made to him to that effect and he had to retire prematurely, although he was still capable of working hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And in his work in 1992, in the 4th Detachment, he was responsible for matters relating to security and intelligence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And again, that was another reason that made it imperative for him to have the clearest and best possible picture of the plans and policies and intentions of the national parties, including the SDS?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was worried. He probably had a lot of information about the work of the SDS and the work of the SDS, and of the HDZ and the SDA, the national parties, that cooperated before the war, during the war and at the present day, they agree amongst themselves very well. We do not belong to these parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And so developments in February and March of 1992, when the SDS was instrumental in declaring a Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac, was a matter that was obviously extremely well known to your husband, and you as well?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I didn't find all of this very clear. I was born in Bosanski Samac. I lived in Bosanski Samac, and all of a sudden, overnight, this Samac is no longer Bosanski Samac. It's just Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. It's uncontested that in February and March of 1992, the SDS was instrumental in setting up a Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac, they held meetings, they appointed people to various positions. Did your husband ever discuss that development with you?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: We talked about many things. He was always unsatisfied. The concept of the 4th Detachment was to safeguard all the citizens in the town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Zaric, but what I'm really interested in was -- is this: That's the announcement in February and March of 1992, of the creation of a Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac. Was that topic ever the subject of discussion between you and your husband?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you aware of the appointment of various people to various posts in this new Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac? For example, the appointment of Stevan Todorovic as police chief?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that a matter that was well known throughout Bosanski Samac or was it not so well known?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I may just have one correction, it would be much more helpful if we would -- if my colleague would ask the witness when she learned about that, that Stevan Todorovic was appointed as Chief of Police. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly, I'm happy to oblige Mr. Lazarevic if he wants that question asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did you find out about the appointment of Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I found out about that in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Pre or post 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: After the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. We'll leave that topic and move on to another one. You mentioned in your evidence a telephone call that took place late on the 16th of April, in which your husband spoke with Luka Gregurevic. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And your husband, after the phone call, told you what had been said?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: One of the things he said was that men had been -- men had been seen walking around Tisina with white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That night, the -- at about that time, late, on the 16th, before midnight, your husband was at home, not obviously not engaged -- obviously not engaged in any 4th Detachment activities of any particular importance?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you're not aware of the 4th Detachment being on any particular manoeuvres at about that time on late on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't think that any such thing was going on, because if it were, Simo would have been with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: With respect that makes sense, doesn't it? All right. So these men with white ribbons were not -- couldn't have been or very unlikely to have been members of the 4th Detachment in Tisina?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The men who came to your apartment and sought weapons, were they wearing white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You stayed in the town until, I think, the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No. Until the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. 21st. Did you see in that period of time any members of the 4th Detachment wearing white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I did not leave the house at all throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. When your husband came home in that period of time, whenever it may have been, during the day or at night, was he wearing a white ribbon?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. No, no, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's move to another topic. You said that Mr. Zaric, your husband, explained to you that a Crisis Staff was being formed. You recall giving that evidence this morning?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did he provide you with that information?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: This was on the following day or -- the 17th, rather, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thank you. After his return from Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in fact, he gave you a little more information than simply a Crisis Staff had been formed. Isn't it the case that he came home and told you that a police station had been occupied by some paramilitary formations and police?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that vital facilities in Bosanski Samac had been taken by the police, and the paramilitary formations that had come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And that buildings had been occupied? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know which buildings you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, no. The buildings aren't important. Did he tell you, did your husband tell you, that some buildings had been occupied by these paramilitary formations and the police?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that the vital facilities in Bosanski Samac, the police station, and the other vital facilities, were taken over, occupied, by the paramilitary formations in cooperation with the police, the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And did he also tell you that a government was being set up by a Serbian -- Serbian Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition, it wasn't just your husband who had access to that information but also other people in the building?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: We gathered at the entrance and somebody had always heard something, somebody would go out to get bread and they would find out about things. Some of this was misinformation but some of it was genuine information. However, I didn't dare go out. I was afraid. I was in the apartment all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Your husband did not mention anything to the effect that the 4th Detachment was going to remove this paramilitary group, did he?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your husband did not mention anything to the effect that the 4th Detachment was going to liberate the police station from the seizure by this paramilitary group, did he?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness decidedly said that she did not know anything about the information that her husband collected and he said -- and she said that it was highly confidential, highly secret, so this line of questioning isn't leading us anywhere. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm asking what Mr. Zaric said to this witness or what he did not say to this witness, words that he did or did not utter. It's a pure question of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio is right. You can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He did not say anything to you to the effect that the 4th Detachment was going to remove this illegal Serbian municipality, this new administration? Sorry, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What he did explain to you, however, was that the 4th Detachment was going to set up positions on the river banks and guard those river banks which face Croatia, well, at least the Sava, the Sava does?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And to protect from any outside attack, that's what he did say to you?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. In the period of time up until the 21st, when you eventually left for Belgrade, the new civilian authorities in Bosanski Samac started to consolidate their power, did they not, by declaring curfews, introducing state of emergency, and various other edicts and decrees?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just returning for one moment to the conversation I was asking you about earlier, when your husband told you that positions were going to be taken up on the Sava and the Bosna, did he also mention to you anything about the intended collection of weapons?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, it's 10.30, it's time for our break, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break and come back at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaric, I was asking you about the consolidation of power by the new civilian authorities and you told us that they introduced a state of emergency and did other things, such as imposing curfews and strengthening their grip on power, correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In addition, were you able to see from your home, or indeed anywhere in Bosanski Samac or did you hear of paramilitaries going about the town seizing weapons?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And this was apparent to you even before you left Bosanski Samac, even before the 21st, that that's what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Plainly what they were doing was also participating in the seizure of power?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At the same time that this seizure of power was going on, the 4th Detachment, as far as you could tell, was setting up its positions on the embankments of the Sava and Bosna rivers?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I know Simo told me the next day that the 4th Detachment has set its position on the embankment of the Sava River and in the evening these Special Forces came into Samac. This is what Simo told me, together with the police. And only the next day did the 4th Detachment set its positions along the Sava River. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just a bit concerned about your sequence, okay? Tell me if this is correct: On the night of the 16th and 17th, the commencement of the seizure of power began, which involved the paramilitaries coming in, the seizure of buildings and so on. Then on the 17th, during the day, the 4th Detachment started setting up its positions? Is that a -- is that the correct sequence?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And the seizure -- sorry, the collection, if you -- call it what you will, of weapons by the 4th Detachment, the part that you saw, that happened on the 18th, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you concerned that the 4th Detachment was assisting this seizure of power by its actions in setting up positions on the embankment and collecting weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. I object to this question, concerned that stating that the 4th Detachment assisted the seizure of power. This is not what this witness could answer. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was assisting the seizure of power by setting up this perimeter around the town and by collecting weapons from the citizenry. That's correct, or am I incorrect?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I think that this is not correct. This is not the way I see it. If they stood by the River Sava, which we are actually bordering the Republic of Croatia, so they were -- they were protecting Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is Bosanski Samac, from another country, now, the extent to which they could actually help people, well probably they could only help those people who remained in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. They may -- your position is that they were defending the town, the -- from attack from another country. However, they did nothing, did they, to remove the insurgents in the town, the paramilitaries and this new Serbian Crisis Staff that has -- that had taken power?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what else they could have done, even they -- if they had raised their voice against it, I don't think anyone of them would have remained alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever get an idea of how many paramilitaries there were in the town? This is in the period of time between the 17th and 21st, when you left.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: We all called them by the same name, we called them the many-coloured, because we -- they stopped me, they asked me to -- they asked us to look at the car, and this was terrible for me. This was already before the war, and I didn't know who they were. Afterwards, it transpired, actually it turned out, it became quite clear what sort of an evil they represented. They were prepared to do everything, to kill, to rape, and who knows what else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fair enough but did you have any idea between the 17th and the 21st, when you left, of the numbers of sareni or paramilitaries who had come into the town, the numbers who had been involved in the takeover?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you aware who brought in these paramilitaries or sareni and the Serbian police who took over the town?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I heard, I read about it, that they were brought by Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But apart from your subsequent readings in that period of time between the 17th and the 21st, did you obtain from anywhere, any information of who was involved in bringing in these paramilitaries and Serbian police to accomplish this takeover?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. You described an episode in your evidence this morning of an occasion when your husband complained of an episode where a gun had been pushed into his mouth and how he had been humiliated and so on. You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You made the comment that this was done by people who wanted to destroy everything?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that something that your husband told you?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, he did talk about them in the -- as the worst people, it was at the time while I was still there, that they were the ones who dominated everything in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I realise that this is -- these are events that took place 11 years ago, it's a long time ago, and that they're emotional times and that your recollection cannot be absolutely precise?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But what I'm interested in is this: Did your husband make it clear to you that his view was that these people wanted to destroy everything when he was talking to you about the episode of the gun in the mouth?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And by that, he meant the destruction of the existing ethnic order, the destruction of the existing institutions, the destruction of coexistence? Is that how you understood his comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I may, okay. Now it's all right, because when I read the last sentence of the question, now it's all right. I wanted to object. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Am I correct that when he said that these were people who wanted to destroy everything, he was talking about people who wanted to destroy the institutions of ethnic tolerance and togetherness? Is that a fair summary of how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. They would not accept coexistence and whoever decided to oppose them would end up in jail, perhaps even be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I've got no quarrel with that. I understand that but what I'm asking you is this: When your husband spoke to you, when he came back after that emotional episode, and he said these are people who want to destroy everything, you understood him to be talking about the destruction of existing institutions that allowed for ethnic tolerance and cohabitation?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Precisely. MR. DI FAZIO: Again will Your Honours just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So -- and when he spoke about these people, he was talking, wasn't he, as far as you could tell, about all of the people involved in the seizure of power, the Serbian Crisis Staff, the paramilitaries, the Serbian police, all of them who were acting together to take over control of the town?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I -- the witness already answered but I believe that it was unfair question for this witness because first he referred to the paramilitaries and the event that Mr. Zaric had with paramilitaries and Mr. Todorovic who threatened him and she understood after this event that Mr. Zaric when talking about this -- referring to this, to this person, so to Mr. Todorovic and the paramilitaries. Now the witness is asking about others taking control of the town so maybe this could be clarified, what -- who are the persons that Mr. Zaric was referring when he talked to his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, I think Mr. Lazarevic is right to the extent that the other people included -- the other institutions included in your question could have misled the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: If you just give me a moment to read the transcript, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: M'hm. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me ask you this way. When your husband said these people want to destroy everything, who did you understand him to be talking about?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: I meant non-Serbs, people who wanted to live together, who are honest, who were in favour of cohabitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, perhaps I've -- my question wasn't that clear. I'll try again. What I meant was when your husband told you, came back and said to you these people want to destroy everything --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What people was he talking about?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, if they arrested only Muslims and Croats, and took them to jail, sometimes they would even take a Serb who was disobedient. I guess he was referring to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he make any reference, when he was talking about the destruction of everything and talking about these issues, to the Serb -- the new Serb Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: He wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff, so that he didn't have anything to talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, no. I understand that. All I'm interested in is your understanding of what he meant when he told you that there were people who wanted to destroy everything or said words to that effect, okay? Who was he talking about? Was he talking about just the paramilitaries? Was he talking about the Serb Crisis Staff? The new civilian administration? Or you don't know? If you don't know, tell us but see if you can clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, he -- it was Stevan Todorovic who was very rude to him and his paramilitaries, and then he said, well, they will destroy everything, and he meant including himself, and that's what he said. He disagreed with them. He didn't know them. He didn't know who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you of his appointment by the Serb Crisis Staff as the director of national security? I believe it was appointment he held for --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You know nothing of that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you approve of his working in any position offered to him by the Serbian Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Di Fazio. That's not a fair question for the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. I'll withdraw it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your husband gave a statement to officers of the OTP on June the 3rd, 1998. And in that statement, he said that Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic brought the paramilitaries into Bosanski Samac. Did he ever give you any such information at any time now, not just between the 17th and the 21st. At any time did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: We didn't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you've got no reason to disbelieve him when he makes that assertion, have you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, again, that's not a fair question. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one last topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Di Fazio, you have to remember that this witness is no ordinary witness, she is the wife of the accused. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm very mindful of that, Your Honours and I've cut my questions short every time that you have indicated, I have no problem with that at all, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your brother, I think, is Fadil Topcagic, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to speak to him between the 16th and the -- sorry, between the 17th and the 21st of April, when you left?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: We didn't meet at all. We didn't see each other at the time at all. I tried to reach him on the phone but there was nobody at his house, and we didn't see each other at the time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. He was in the 4th Detachment. Do you know what position he held in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZARIC
utterances.text: He was just a private, a soldier like any other. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Zaric, for giving evidence. We are finished with you. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, our last information is that three of our witnesses have left Bosanski Samac yesterday, arrived in Belgrade, and we don't have so far any information whether they have arrived in The Hague. They should have been here by now, but there is no information from witness and -- Victims and Witnesses Section. So at this point, I believe we have no any witness for today. Hopefully -- well, what I can assure the Trial Chamber is that tomorrow we will have three witnesses who arrive -- who I hope will have arrived this morning in The Hague, and I can give the order of their appearance for the Trial Chamber right now. First witness would be Sekulic, Stoko. After him, witness Arnautovic, Jusuf. And then after him, witness Omeranovic, Mustafa. Witness Tihic, Pasaga will come in The Hague on Saturday and he will be ready to give his testimony on Monday, together with some other witnesses, and we will inform the Trial Chamber as soon as we can. And these are all four witnesses -- all these four witnesses were supposed to give their testimony by the way of Rule 71 but the Trial Chamber decided to call them here and to hear their testimony viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, so that we can observe them, yes. Yes. So do please keep the legal officer informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have already seen her an hour ago and I promised -- made that promise to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have you checked your documents, the ones Judge Lindholm had raised yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. We have verified it yesterday. These documents were not admitted into evidence, the ones that Honourable Judge Lindholm asked about. We intended to tender these but have actually decided to withdraw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other matters before we rise? No? MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall rise and continue our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 11.28 a.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 4th day of April, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
